analysis.one_liner: Cuts the estate tax rate to 30% and shields the first $10 million of an estate from tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the top estate and gift tax rate to a flat 30%, exempted the first $10 million of any estate from taxation (with that amount rising with inflation), and raised the amount a person can give away each year tax-free from $10,000 to $50,000. Estate taxes only apply to very large inheritances, so the money would have gone almost entirely to heirs of the wealthiest families, while reducing federal revenue that otherwise funds government services. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth more than $10 million, who would pay a 30% rate instead of the much higher graduated rates then in law, and wealthy families making large annual tax-free gifts. Estate-planning lawyers and advisors would also gain a larger but simplified market.

how_it_helps.text: It replaces the graduated estate tax — which rose well above 30% on large taxable estates — with a flat 30% rate [S3].
It raises the unified credit's exclusion equivalent to $10 million and indexes it to inflation, so estates under that size would owe no estate tax at all [S3].

It raises the annual gift tax exclusion from $10,000 to $50,000 per recipient, letting wealthy families transfer money to relatives each year without touching their lifetime exemption or paying gift tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, because estate tax revenue — which in 2003 applied only to a small share of very large estates — would have shrunk, leaving less money for government programs or forcing other taxes to make up the difference.

drawbacks.text: The revenue cost would fall on everyone else: the estate tax applies only to large estates, so eliminating most of it is a targeted tax cut for the wealthiest families funded by the broader tax base [S3].

The $50,000 annual gift exclusion and the $10 million exemption primarily benefit families with substantial assets to transfer; a typical household gives or inherits far less than those thresholds [S3].

Estate tax advocates argue the tax limits the growth of concentrated, inherited wealth across generations; a permanent cut to 30% with a $10 million exemption would have significantly reduced that check on large fortunes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are narrow and real for those who receive them — a family inheriting $20 million would save millions in tax — but the cost is spread across all federal taxpayers through lost revenue, and the bill offered nothing for households without large estates or gifts. On balance it is a targeted transfer toward the wealthiest families.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Leach introduced the bill on June 16, 2003, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law [S1][S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax remained at its 2003 levels and no revenue was lost. Heirs of large estates lost a potential tax break, while the general taxpayer base was spared the cost. With zero cosponsors and no committee action, no group gained from the bill's death beyond the status quo holding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no one gained

for.name: Rep. Jim Leach
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the partisan shape of support never formed [S4].

industries.note: Had it passed, families with estates over $10 million would have saved substantial tax, and the $50,000 annual gift exclusion would have eased large intergenerational transfers. Because it died, they gained nothing.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisors
industries.note: A lower rate and a $10 million exemption would have shrunk the need for estate tax planning, though the higher gift exclusion would have created some new planning work.
